title: Erik Davis on Philip K. Dick and Sonic Youth (SPIN, January 1989) — quotation excerpts
author: Erik Davis (Thurston Moore quoted)
card_summary: Excerpted quotations from Erik Davis's January 1989 SPIN magazine article on Philip K. Dick's influence on Sonic Youth, plus Thurston Moore quotes from Alec Foege's Confusion is Next: The Sonic Youth Story (St. Martin's Press, 1994, pp. 162–163). Documents PKD's reception in 1980s American alternative rock, including the 'Schizophrenia' song from Sister (1987) and the album title's reference to PKD's lost twin sister Jane.
page_summary:
Excerpted quotations documenting Philip K. Dick's reception in 1980s American alternative rock, specifically the influence on Sonic Youth's mid-period work (Sister, 1987; Daydream Nation, 1988). The source documents are: (1) Erik Davis's January 1989 SPIN magazine article on PKD and Sonic Youth, in which Davis writes of how 'when Dick wrote in Valis that the symbols of the divine show up at the trash stratum, he was anticipating Sonic Youth's lyrics, which mix in religious and occult imagery with their scuzzy skanking for pop and violence. The stuff is powerful enough to set off Dick's kind of spiritual paranoia'; (2) Thurston Moore quotes in SPIN and in Alec Foege's Confusion is Next: The Sonic Youth Story (St. Martin's Press, 1994, pp. 162–163), in which Moore acknowledges PKD as the central literary influence on his lyrics during the Sister-Daydream Nation period: 'You didn't really have to read Kant or Hegel or the Bible or other things — you could read Philip K. Dick and get a lot of ideas through one writer. ... I always liked the idea that writing lyrics was more of a subconscious attitude, in a way. It really came to fruition while reading Philip K. Dick for a couple of years, and also while writing Sister.' Moore's characterization of PKD: 'He was very well read, but he writes in common speech, not like an academic. Dick was really compulsive. He'd change his mind all the time. ... Schizophrenia's just another word for cosmology.'

Documentary value: (1) the album Sister (1987) takes its title from PKD's lost twin sister Jane (per Foege, p. 163), making Sonic Youth's most-celebrated mid-period album a sustained engagement with PKD's biographical material; (2) the album's opener 'Schizophrenia' takes lyrical cues from Radio Free Albemuth and VALIS, the late tetralogy filtered through Moore's reading; (3) Davis's article is the canonical short essay on PKD and rock music, predating the academic-scholarly treatment of PKD's reception in popular culture; (4) the Foege biography preserves Moore's testimony in book form and remains the primary source for Sonic Youth's PKD engagement.

Reception position: Sonic Youth's PKD engagement has been cited in subsequent academic and fan-academic accounts of PKD's cultural reception (David Gill's MA thesis, 2006; PKD Otaku; Total Dick-Head). Davis would later write more sustained PKD scholarship (TechGnosis, 1998; High Weirdness, 2019; the Exegesis annotations), and the SPIN article is the genealogical origin of his subsequent professional engagement with PKD.
